sub: Named after al-Kawthar, “abundant good”, in ayah 1
theme: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ when enemies mocked him as “cut off” after his sons died. Allah has given him abundant good, so he should pray and sacrifice for Allah; his hater is the one cut off.
story: The shortest surah in the Quran. Most say it came in Makkah, in a hard period; others say Madinah, because the Prophet ﷺ once woke from a doze smiling and said a surah had just been revealed to him.

Arabs called a man whose sons had died abtar, “cut off”. When the Prophet’s ﷺ son died, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil reportedly said: “Leave him, he is cut off. When he dies, no one will remember him.” Other reports name Abū Lahab, Abū Jahl or ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ.
Another report says Quraysh asked Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf whether they were better than this man “cut off from his people”, and he said they were. The surah answers all of them.

sections.title: Abundance for you; your enemy cut off
sections.meaning: Allah has given the Prophet ﷺ al-Kawthar: abundant good, including a river in Paradise and the Pool his followers will drink from. In thanks he should pray and sacrifice for his Lord alone. The one who hates him is the one cut off from all good.
points: We have given you al-Kawthar, abundant good
So pray to your Lord and sacrifice
Your hater is the one cut off
sections.matters: It turns an insult upside down. They said his name would die with his sons. Instead his name is honoured across the world and his way followed until the end of time, while his mockers are forgotten.
sections.story: When the Prophet’s ﷺ sons died, his enemies called him abtar, a man with no son to carry his name. Most reports name al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil; others name Abū Lahab, Abū Jahl, ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, or Quraysh with Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf.
explained: Al-Kawthar comes from kathrah, abundance: abundant good in this world and the next. Part of that good is a river in Paradise, whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, and the Pool on the Day of Judgement, with cups as many as the stars.

Fa-ṣalli li-rabbika wa-nḥar: make your prayer and your sacrifice for your Lord alone, unlike idol-worshippers who bowed and slaughtered for others. Shāniʾaka: whoever hates you. Huwa al-abtar: he is the one cut off from every good, his name and deeds forgotten.
teaches: Allah’s gifts outweigh anything people take from you or say about you.
Answer blessings with prayer and sacrifice for Allah alone.
Mockery cannot erase what Allah raises.
Hating the Prophet ﷺ and his message leads only to loss.
sections.hook: Three short ayat, three steps: a gift (innā aʿṭaynāka), a response (fa-ṣalli), a verdict (inna shāniʾaka). Ayat 1 and 3 both open with inna.

groups.text: Allah has given you abundant good, so pray and sacrifice for your Lord alone.
The one who hates you is the one truly cut off.

1.explain: Innā aʿṭaynāka al-kawthar: We have given you abundant good. It includes a river in Paradise and the Pool where his followers will come to drink on the Day of Judgement.
1.why: The Prophet ﷺ dozed, then raised his head smiling and said a surah had just been revealed to him. He recited it and said al-Kawthar is a river his Lord promised him, full of good.

2.explain: In thanks, make your prayer and your sacrifice for your Lord alone, unlike idol-worshippers who prayed and slaughtered for others. Some link it to the Eid prayer and the sacrifice that follows.

3.explain: Shāniʾaka: whoever hates you and what you brought. Al-abtar: cut off from all good, with no lasting name. The mocker, not the Prophet ﷺ, is the one cut off.
3.why: When the Prophet’s ﷺ son died, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil reportedly said: “Leave him, he is abtar; when he dies he will be forgotten.” Other reports name Abū Lahab, Abū Jahl, ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, or Quraysh speaking to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf.
